cases.title: An order total that drifts
cases.briefMd: An order keeps a running total so checkout doesn't add up every item again. The cart page reads the items to show them.
cases.explanationMd:
Returning the internal list hands callers the object itself, so `order.getItems().add(x)` or `.clear()` changes the items without touching `totalCents`, and the total drifts. That breaks **encapsulation**: a class can only keep its rule (the total equals the sum of the items) if every change goes through its own methods.

Return a read-only view (`Collections.unmodifiableList(items)`) or a copy (`List.copyOf(items)`). The same idea in Python is returning a tuple or a copy, and in C++ returning `const std::vector<Item>&`.

cases.title: A label that crashes while being built
cases.briefMd: A base `Widget` draws itself as soon as it's created. `new Label("hi")` throws a NullPointerException.
cases.explanationMd:
`Widget`'s constructor calls `render()`, which `Label` overrides. Java runs the base constructor *before* the subclass constructor body, so `Label.render()` runs while `text` is still `null`, and `text.toUpperCase()` throws.

Don't call overridable methods from a constructor: finish building the object, then draw it (`new Label("hi").show()`), or make the method `final` or `private`. C++ has the same trap in a different shape (a virtual call in a constructor runs the *base* version), and so does Python when a parent's `__init__` calls a method the child overrides.

cases.title: A stack you can reach into
cases.briefMd: The undo stack of an editor: only the most recent action may be undone.
choices: Extending `ArrayList` makes the stack *be* a list: callers can still call `add(0, x)`, `remove(3)` or `set(i, x)` and break last-in-first-out. Wrap a private list instead.
`pop()` is O(n) because `remove` shifts every element to the left.
It should extend `LinkedList`, because an `ArrayList` can't grow past its first capacity.
A generic class can't extend a concrete generic type like `ArrayList<T>`.
cases.explanationMd:
Inheritance says *a Stack is an ArrayList*, so every public list method comes along: `add(0, x)`, `remove(3)`, `set(i, x)`, `clear()`. Any caller can reorder or edit the middle of the history, and the stack can't stop it. (`java.util.Stack extends Vector` has exactly this flaw, which is why `ArrayDeque` is recommended instead.)

**Favour composition over inheritance**: keep a private list and expose only push, pop and peek. Inherit when the child really can be used everywhere the parent is; reuse code by holding an object, not by becoming one.

fixed: private final ArrayList<T> items = new ArrayList<>();

cases.title: A square that won't stay a rectangle
cases.briefMd: Shapes for a layout engine. `stretch` resizes any rectangle it's given.
choices: `Square` breaks Liskov substitution: code written for `Rectangle` expects width and height to change independently, so `stretch(Square(3))` ends with area 25, not 50.
`Square.__init__` must call `super().__init__(side)` with a single argument.
`area` has to be a `@property`, or subclasses can't override it.
Python never calls a subclass's override from a parent-typed parameter, so `Square.set_width` is never used.
cases.explanationMd:
The **Liskov substitution principle** (the L in SOLID): a subclass must work anywhere its parent is expected. Code written for `Rectangle` relies on "setting the width leaves the height alone", and `Square` can't keep that promise: `stretch(Square(3))` ends with a 5×5 square, area 25, and the assert fails.

A square *is* a rectangle in geometry, but a **mutable** square isn't a substitute for a mutable rectangle. Make them siblings under a common `Shape`, or make shapes immutable so there are no setters to break.

cases.title: Every new shape edits the same functions
cases.briefMd: Geometry helpers for a drawing app that adds a shape every sprint. Triangles are next.
choices: Adding a shape means editing every `isinstance` chain, and a missed one only fails at runtime. Give each shape its own `area()` and `perimeter()` methods instead (polymorphism, open/closed).
`isinstance` doesn't work for classes defined in the same module; compare `type(shape).__name__` instead.
3.14159 isn't precise enough, so areas are wrong in the third decimal.
The functions should return `None` for unknown shapes instead of raising `TypeError`.
cases.explanationMd:
Each function asks "which kind of shape is this?" and handles every kind itself. Adding `Triangle` means finding and editing every such chain (area, perimeter, and whatever comes later), and a missed one only fails at runtime with `TypeError`.

The **open/closed principle**: code should be open for extension (add a class) and closed for modification (no edits to working code). Put the behaviour on the shapes, so each class implements `area()` and `perimeter()` (**polymorphism**), and adding a triangle touches nothing else. (`math.pi` is nicer than 3.14159, but that's not the design problem.)

cases.title: A checkout that knows every wallet
cases.briefMd: Takes payment for an order. Apple Pay and bank transfers are on the roadmap.
choices: Each new payment method edits `Checkout`, and every branch builds its own client so none can be swapped in tests. Use a `PaymentMethod` interface with one class per method (Strategy), looked up by name.
Comparing strings with `equals` is too slow for a checkout path; use `==`.
`IllegalArgumentException` is unchecked, so callers won't know they have to catch it.
The method should be `static`, because `Checkout` has no fields.
cases.explanationMd:
Every payment method lives inside `Checkout`: adding Apple Pay means editing this method again, re-testing all the others, and each branch builds its own client, so none of them can be replaced by a fake in tests.

This is what the **Strategy** pattern is for: one `PaymentMethod` interface, one class per method (card, PayPal, gift card), and `Checkout` picks one by name from a map it's given. New methods are new classes; `Checkout` doesn't change (open/closed). A **factory** can build the map from configuration.

cases.title: Widgets that never go away
cases.briefMd: A dashboard opens and closes many `PriceWidget`s, all listening to one app-wide `PriceFeed` (it has `addListener` and `removeListener`). After a day, memory keeps growing and closed widgets still print prices.
cases.explanationMd:
The classic **Observer** pitfall, the *lapsed listener*. The feed lives as long as the app and keeps a reference to every widget that subscribed, so a closed widget can never be garbage-collected and keeps receiving updates.

Whatever subscribes must unsubscribe: `close()` calls `feed.removeListener(this)`. Other fixes are a `Subscription` handle returned by `addListener` with a `cancel()` method, or weak references in the subject.

cases.title: A store that forgets every write
cases.briefMd: Production wraps the real key-value store in a `LoggingStore` to trace calls. Since it shipped, a value written a moment ago reads back as missing.
cases.explanationMd:
A **decorator** adds behaviour around another object with the same interface, and it has to pass every call on to the object it wraps. `put` logs and stops there, so writes never reach the real store.

Forward the call: `self.inner.put(key, value)`. When an interface has many methods it's easy to miss one; a base decorator that forwards everything by default (or `__getattr__` delegation in Python) means each decorator only overrides what it changes.

cases.title: Undo that wipes the page
cases.briefMd: A text editor built on commands so every action can be undone. Type "ab", then "c", press undo, and the whole document is gone.
cases.explanationMd:
In the **Command** pattern each command knows how to do and undo exactly its own change. `InsertText.undo` resets the whole document instead of removing the text it added, so undoing the last keystroke erases everything typed before it.

Remove only what was appended: `self.doc.text = self.doc.text[: len(self.doc.text) - len(self.s)]`. When the inverse isn't easy to compute (deleting a selection, reformatting), the command saves what it needs during `execute` (a small **memento**) and restores it in `undo`.

cases.title: Which number was the timeout?
cases.briefMd: An HTTP client with sensible defaults. In production, calls to the API time out after 3 seconds and are retried 30 times.
choices: Telescoping constructors: five positional arguments with two `int`s and two `boolean`s side by side, so swapping timeout and retries still compiles. A Builder with named steps makes each value say what it is.
A Java constructor can't call another constructor with `this(...)`.
The class needs a no-argument constructor so frameworks can create it.
The `boolean` parameters should be `Boolean`, so callers can pass `null` for the default.
cases.explanationMd:
These are **telescoping constructors**: each overload adds a parameter, and the full one takes five positional arguments, two `int`s and two `boolean`s next to each other. The caller swapped timeout and retries, and it compiles fine. Defaults are also repeated across overloads.

A **Builder** names every value at the call site (`.timeoutSec(30).retries(3)`), keeps defaults in one place, and lets you add options without new constructors. (Java records and Python keyword arguments solve the same problem in other ways.)

cases.title: Read once, read everywhere
cases.briefMd: Configuration is meant to be read from disk once and shared through `AppConfig.get()`. Profiling shows `app.properties` being read hundreds of times a minute.
cases.explanationMd:
A **Singleton** only works if nobody else can create the object. With a public constructor, any code can write `new AppConfig()`, and each one reads the file again and holds its own copy, which is exactly what the profile shows.

Make the constructor `private` so `get()` is the only way in. Then consider whether it should be a singleton at all: global state hides dependencies and makes tests share configuration. Many teams create one `AppConfig` at startup and pass it to whoever needs it (dependency injection).

cases.title: A printer that has to pretend to fax
cases.briefMd: Drivers for office devices. Most models only print; a few also scan and fax.
choices: One fat interface makes every device implement features it doesn't have, so callers only find out at runtime. Split it into small interfaces (Printer, Scanner, Fax) and implement just what each device supports.
Interface methods can't take two parameters, so `fax` won't compile.
`UnsupportedOperationException` is a checked exception, so every caller must catch it.
`BasicPrinter` has to be `abstract`, because it doesn't support every method.
cases.explanationMd:
One large interface forces every device to implement everything, so `BasicPrinter` "supports" scanning and faxing by throwing. Callers can't tell from the type what will work; they find out at runtime.

The **interface segregation principle** (the I in SOLID): many small interfaces beat one big one. Split it into `Printer`, `DocScanner` and `Fax`, and let each device implement only what it can do. A method that needs to fax takes a `Fax`, and the compiler stops you passing a plain printer.

cases.title: Everyone's cart has everything
cases.briefMd: One `Cart` per signed-in user. After launch, users see items they never added.
cases.explanationMd:
Names assigned in the class body belong to the **class**, so they're shared by every instance. `self.items.append(...)` finds the single class-level list and changes it for every cart.

Per-object state belongs in `__init__` (`self.items = []`). `discount = 0` is harmless: numbers can't be changed in place, and `self.discount = 5` creates an attribute on that one cart. Java and C++ make the same distinction explicit with `static`.

cases.title: Half a sensor gets cleaned up
cases.briefMd: Every call to `poll()` leaks 2 MB, although `Camera` frees its buffer in its destructor.
cases.explanationMd:
Deleting a `Camera` through a `Sensor*` only runs `~Camera` if `Sensor`'s destructor is **virtual**; otherwise it's undefined behaviour, and in practice only the base part is destroyed, so the frame buffer leaks.

A class meant to be used through a base pointer needs `virtual ~Sensor() = default;`. Better still, let members clean up after themselves: hold the buffer in a `std::vector<unsigned char>` and the sensor in a `std::unique_ptr<Sensor>`, and no hand-written destructor or `delete` is needed (RAII).

cases.title: Every animal says "..."
cases.briefMd: A zoo of animals, each with its own sound. The program prints "..." twice.
cases.explanationMd:
`std::vector<Animal>` stores `Animal` **values**. `push_back(Dog{})` copies only the `Animal` part of the dog into the vector (**object slicing**), so the stored objects really are plain Animals and `sound()` returns "...".

Polymorphism in C++ needs a pointer or reference to the real object: store `std::unique_ptr<Animal>` (or another smart pointer) and create each animal with `std::make_unique<Dog>()`. Java and Python never slice, because every object variable there is already a reference.

lines: for (const Animal& a : zoo) std::cout << a.sound() << "\n";
fixed: for (const auto& a : zoo) std::cout << a->sound() << "\n";

cases.title: A car that parks itself
cases.briefMd: Object-oriented design for a multi-level parking garage: motorcycles, cars and vans, spots in three sizes, pay by card on exit. The interviewer will add EV charging spots next.
cases.explanationMd:
`Vehicle.park()` gives a car four jobs: searching the garage, managing spot state, taking payment and printing tickets. A vehicle shouldn't know how the garage is laid out or how payments work (**single responsibility**, low coupling), and charging at entry duplicates the payment that `exit` already does.

The lot owns its spots, so `ParkingLot.park(vehicle)` finds and reserves a spot and returns a Ticket; payment stays in one place. Adding EV spots then means a new spot type and a change to the lot's search, with every vehicle class untouched.

cases.title: Sixteen ways to be in four states
cases.briefMd: A vending machine: insert coins, pick a product, get the product and change. It can be sold out or in maintenance. The interviewer will add card payments (with a "waiting for the bank" state) next.
cases.explanationMd:
Four booleans allow 16 combinations, most of them meaningless (dispensing *and* in maintenance?), and every method needs an if/else ladder that has to stay consistent as features arrive. Adding "waiting for the bank" means a fifth flag and edits everywhere.

The **State** pattern makes each state a class that decides what each action does and which state comes next. Illegal combinations can't exist, and card payments become one new state class instead of changes to every method.

cases.title: Only one person can read Dune
cases.briefMd: A library system: members search the catalogue, borrow up to 5 items for 3 weeks, reserve items that are out and pay late fees. Popular books have several copies.
cases.explanationMd:
Putting the borrower and due date on `Book` mixes up the *title* with the physical *copy*. With three copies of *Dune* there is still a single `borrower` field, so only one person can have it, and the loan history disappears when it comes back.

Separate the catalogue entry (Book) from the items on the shelf (BookCopy), and record each borrowing as its own object (Loan). This split between a kind of thing and its instances comes up in most OOD interviews: movies and showings, flights and seats, products and stock items.

Fines: a FinePolicy computes the late fee from the due date and the return date.
Notifications: a Notifier sends due-date reminders and reservation alerts by email or SMS.

cases.title: WhatsApp means editing everything
cases.briefMd: A notification service: users choose email, SMS or push for each kind of notification. Product wants WhatsApp and Slack next quarter.
choices: Every new channel means editing NotificationService (a new branch and a new method). Define a Channel interface with one class per provider and look them up in a registry.
Templates should be rendered after the retries, so a retry can pick up a newer template.
Quiet hours should apply to urgent notifications too, for consistency.
Preferences should be per user only, not per notification type, to keep the table small.
cases.explanationMd:
Branching on the channel name puts every provider's details in one class. Each new channel edits `NotificationService`, its tests grow with every provider, and a bug in the SMS branch can ship with the WhatsApp change.

Make channels pluggable (the **Strategy** pattern, open/closed principle): a `Channel` interface with one class per provider, registered by name. WhatsApp becomes one new class plus a registry entry, while retries, quiet hours and auditing stay shared.

Share behaviour without inheritance: a `slide` helper with direction lists, used by Rook, Bishop and Queen, and fixed step lists for King and Knight. Each piece stays a direct subclass of `Piece`.

cases.title: A room booked forever
cases.briefMd: A hotel booking system: guests search rooms by date range and type, book, cancel, check in and check out. Rooms are booked months ahead.
cases.explanationMd:
One boolean can't describe a calendar. A room booked for next July is "booked" today too, so nobody can book it for tonight, and a cancellation flips it back for everyone.

Availability depends on reservations over time: a room is free for a range when no active reservation overlaps it (`start < requestedEnd && end > requestedStart`). Storing state on an entity that should be **derived** from the records that own the truth is a common OOD mistake.

cases.title: A logger nobody can swap
cases.briefMd: Logging for a backend with 200 classes. Tests need to check what was logged, and production wants JSON logs shipped to a log service.
choices: Every class grabs one global, file-bound instance, so tests can't capture logs and moving to JSON or a log service changes everyone's dependency. Pass in a Logger interface with pluggable sinks.
The background writer thread should go: writing synchronously is always faster.
Rotation should be weekly, to keep fewer files.
Thread names don't belong in log lines, because they change between runs.
cases.explanationMd:
A singleton is global state and a hidden dependency: nothing in a class's constructor says it logs, and all 200 classes are wired to one file-writing implementation. That's why tests can't capture log lines without touching the real file, and why switching to JSON or a log service is a change to everyone's dependency.

Depend on an abstraction and pass it in (**dependency inversion**): a `Logger` interface with pluggable sinks. Real logging libraries (SLF4J, Python's `logging`) work this way, with a logger per class from a factory and handlers chosen by configuration.

Format: plain text lines with timestamp, level, thread name and message.

Performance: log calls go on an in-memory queue that a background thread writes out.

cases.title: Two elevators answer one button
cases.briefMd: An elevator system for a 30-floor office with 6 elevators. People press up or down on a floor (hall calls) and pick a floor inside (car calls).
cases.explanationMd:
With elevators grabbing calls from a shared list, two can claim the same call (both arrive, one trip wasted), or a far-away idle car beats one that is about to pass the floor. Nothing owns the decision, and the scheduling policy is smeared across six objects racing each other.

Give the decision to one object: a **Dispatcher** (controller) assigns each hall call to exactly one elevator using a cost function (distance, direction, load). Scheduling policy lives in one place and can be swapped (Strategy), and elevators simply work through their own queues.

lines: Elevator: a current floor, a direction (up, down, idle), a door state and a queue of stops.
Car calls: buttons inside an elevator add a stop to that elevator's own queue.
Hall calls: go into one shared list; every idle or passing elevator scans it and takes the first call it sees.
Movement: an elevator serves stops in its current direction first, then reverses (the SCAN algorithm).
Capacity: a load sensor stops new pickups when the car is above 90% of its rated weight.
Display: each floor shows where every elevator is and which way it's going.
Emergencies: fire mode sends every elevator to the lobby and ignores calls.
fixed: Elevator: a current floor, a direction (up, down, idle), a door state and a queue of stops.
Car calls: buttons inside an elevator add a stop to that elevator's own queue.
Hall calls: a Dispatcher assigns each hall call to one elevator (the one that can get there soonest), which adds it to its queue.
Movement: an elevator serves stops in its current direction first, then reverses (the SCAN algorithm).
Capacity: a load sensor stops new pickups when the car is above 90% of its rated weight.
Display: each floor shows where every elevator is and which way it's going.
Emergencies: fire mode sends every elevator to the lobby and ignores calls.

cases.title: The missing cent
cases.briefMd: An expense-splitting app: a group adds expenses, splits them equally, by exact amounts or by percentage, and settles up. Balances in a group must always add up to zero.
cases.explanationMd:
$10 split three ways is 3.3333… in floating point: the shares don't add back up to the total, and errors like `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` make balances drift until "settled" groups still show tiny debts.

Money needs an exact representation, integer cents (or `BigDecimal` / `Decimal`) wrapped in a `Money` value object, and an explicit rule for the remainder ($10.00 / 3 = $3.34 + $3.33 + $3.33). Using a raw primitive for a domain concept like money is called **primitive obsession**.

lines: Groups: a Group has members and a list of Expenses.
Expense: payer, total, participants and a SplitStrategy (equal, exact or percentage).
Money: amounts are double values in dollars; an equal share is total / number of participants.
Balances: a Ledger keeps how much each member owes each other member, updated per expense.
Settling up: suggests the fewest payments by matching the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor.
Validation: exact splits must add up to the total, and percentages to 100.
History: expenses can be edited or deleted; the ledger is recomputed from the expense list.
fixed: Groups: a Group has members and a list of Expenses.
Expense: payer, total, participants and a SplitStrategy (equal, exact or percentage).
Money: amounts are integer cents in a Money type; an equal split gives total / n cents each and hands the leftover cents to the first participants.
Balances: a Ledger keeps how much each member owes each other member, updated per expense.
Settling up: suggests the fewest payments by matching the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor.
Validation: exact splits must add up to the total, and percentages to 100.
History: expenses can be edited or deleted; the ledger is recomputed from the expense list.

cases.title: Folders full of special cases
cases.briefMd: An in-memory file system: files and folders, `ls`, `du` (total size), move and delete. Symlinks are the likely follow-up.
choices: Files and directories share no type, so every operation needs two lists and two code paths (and symlinks would add a third). Use the Composite pattern: a Node interface that File and Directory both implement.
resolve should use a regular expression instead of splitting on "/".
Directory.size() should be cached forever after the first call.
ls should list subdirectories before files, like most file managers.
cases.explanationMd:
Files and directories have no common type, so every operation (size, ls, move, delete) needs two lists and two code paths, and a symlink would add a third everywhere.

The **Composite** pattern gives leaves and containers one interface: a `Node` with `size()`, implemented by File and Directory, where a Directory holds child Nodes. Recursive operations collapse to one line (`sum(child.size() for child in children)`), and a new kind of node plugs in without touching the others.

lines: Classes: File has a name, size and contents; Directory has a name, a list of files and a list of subdirectories.
Paths: resolve(path) walks from the root, splitting on "/".
Size: Directory.size() loops over its files, then recursively over its subdirectories.
Listing: ls(path) prints files and subdirectories, sorted by name.
Moving: move(src, dst) removes the entry from its parent and adds it to the destination directory.
Deleting: delete(path) removes a file, or a directory with everything under it.
fixed: Classes: an abstract Node (name, parent, size()); File and Directory extend it, and a Directory holds a list of child Nodes.
Paths: resolve(path) walks from the root, splitting on "/".
Size: File.size() is its length; Directory.size() sums size() over its children without asking what each one is.
Listing: ls(path) prints files and subdirectories, sorted by name.
Moving: move(src, dst) removes the entry from its parent and adds it to the destination directory.
Deleting: delete(path) removes a file, or a directory with everything under it.

cases.title: A fare that reaches through four objects
cases.briefMd: The trip service of a ride-hailing app. Fares depend on the car type (standard, XL, premium), surge, distance and time, and pricing rules change every week.
choices: Trip reaches through driver → car → type → rate plan, so it depends on the internals of four classes (Law of Demeter). A PricingService that takes the car type, distance, time and surge should own the rules.
Surge multipliers should be cached for an hour to cut load.
Matching should offer the ride to every nearby driver at once and take the first to accept.
Ratings should be stored on the Trip object rather than in their own table.
cases.explanationMd:
A chain like `driver.getCar().getType().getRatePlan()` ties `Trip` to the insides of four other classes: change how cars store their type, or where rate plans live, and fare code breaks. The **Law of Demeter** ("only talk to your immediate neighbours") flags exactly this.

Move the knowledge to where it belongs: a `PricingService` that owns the rules and quotes a fare from plain inputs. With pricing changing weekly, that also gives the rules one home that can be tested on its own.

lines: Trip: rider, driver, pickup, drop-off, start and end times, route distance and status.
Matching: a Matcher offers the request to the nearest available drivers, one at a time.
Fare: Trip.fare() computes driver.getCar().getType().getRatePlan().perKm() × km + perMinute × minutes, times surge.
Surge: a SurgeService gives a multiplier per area, cached for one minute.
Payment: the rider's saved method is charged when the trip ends, and a receipt is emailed.
Ratings: rider and driver rate each other after the trip.
fixed: Trip: rider, driver, pickup, drop-off, start and end times, route distance and status.
Matching: a Matcher offers the request to the nearest available drivers, one at a time.
Fare: a PricingService.quote(carType, km, minutes, surge) owns the rate plans; the Trip stores the quote it was given.
Surge: a SurgeService gives a multiplier per area, cached for one minute.
Payment: the rider's saved method is charged when the trip ends, and a receipt is emailed.
Ratings: rider and driver rate each other after the trip.
